title: Why Is DC Not A State?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain why Washington, D.C. is not a state despite roughly 700,000 residents. They trace the history from the Continental Congress and the Compromise of 1790 that placed the capital on the Potomac, through the 1783 Pennsylvania Mutiny that led to a stateless federal district, the 1867 enfranchisement of Black men and its repeal and replacement by a federally appointed commission, and the home rule era with congressional review of local laws and budget riders. They cover the 23rd Amendment giving D.C. electoral votes, the partisan Senate arguments against statehood, proposed workarounds like shrinking the federal district, the Tennessee Plan referendum route, the 2021 House-passed statehood bill that stalled in the Senate, the proposed name Douglass Commonwealth, and how the National Guard control issue shaped the January 6 Capitol attack and the 2020 George Floyd protests. The episode closes with a listener mail shout-out to a baby named Clara.
topics: why DC is not a state

segments.title: Opening and DC's disenfranchisement
segments.summary: Hosts introduce DC statehood, noting about 700,000 residents without full voting representation, the DC license plate 'taxation without representation,' and the question of why DC is not a state.

segments.title: Founding of the capital and the Pennsylvania Mutiny
segments.summary: The Continental Congress moved between cities before the Constitution called for a permanent capital. The Compromise of 1790 placed it farther south, with land ceded by Maryland and Virginia. The 1783 Pennsylvania Mutiny, when veterans confronted Congress and the state militia did not protect it, led the federal government to want a stateless capital with its own jurisdiction.

segments.title: Population growth, home rule, and the 1867 suffrage law
segments.summary: After 1800 DC stayed rural until a post-Civil War population boom brought a majority Black population. Residents pushed for home rule. Congress passed a law in 1867 enfranchising Black men, which was repealed after about three years and replaced by a federally appointed commission. Senator John Tyler Morgan's 'burn down the barn' remark is quoted.

segments.title: Territorial era, non-voting delegate, and congressional review
segments.summary: DC was a territory with a presidentially appointed governor until 1973, with a non-voting delegate in the House and no Senate representation. Under the Home Rule Act, local laws remain subject to congressional review, and riders attached to the budget have blocked DC laws, including a needle exchange program, a sodomy law repeal, and marijuana legalization.

segments.title: Electoral College, 23rd Amendment, and Senate partisanship
segments.summary: DC residents first voted for president in 1961 under the 23rd Amendment, which gives DC electors capped at the smallest state's number, currently three. Electors usually go Democratic. Statehood would add two Democratic senators, which the hosts identify as the core partisan reason for opposition.

segments.title: Arguments against statehood and proposed workarounds
segments.summary: Hosts critique disingenuous arguments: shrinking the federal district to federal buildings, the claim that DC cannot govern federal property, and returning DC to Maryland or Virginia. They discuss constitutional size limits, why a constitutional amendment is a high hurdle, and that all past states were admitted by congressional act. DC's federal funding is about a quarter of its budget and it runs balanced budgets.

segments.title: Tennessee Plan, 2021 House bill, and naming
segments.summary: The Tennessee Plan, used by Michigan, Iowa, California, Oregon, Kansas and Alaska, is a referendum and self-drafted constitution route. DC used it in 2016. A statehood bill passed the House but stalled in the Senate under Mitch McConnell; it was reintroduced and faces Democratic Senate holdouts. The proposed state name is Douglass Commonwealth, honoring Frederick Douglass.

segments.title: January 6 and 2020 protests National Guard
segments.summary: The hosts argue that DC's National Guard is controlled by the federal government, which prevented DC from activating it before January 6, 2021, and led to Guard deployment against George Floyd protesters in 2020.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener mail shout-out to Clara, a baby who listened in the womb, from Karissa Texador. Sign-off.
